THIS IS ABSOLUTELY INSANE.

For the first time in history, a sitting Fed Chair has accused the President of pressuring him to cut interest rates for political reasons.

This is a history book moment because the Federal Reserve is supposed to work independently.

So what is actually happening?

Federal prosecutors sent subpoenas linked to the Fed’s headquarters renovation project.

Officially, it is about construction costs and approvals.

But Powell went public and said, "This is not really about a building. This is about forcing rate cuts.”

That is why markets reacted immediately. The US dollar weakened, Gold pumped.

WHY THIS IS SUCH A BIG DEAL ?

The strength of the US dollar does not only come from the economy. It comes from trust that the system is rule based and stable.

People buy US Treasuries and hold dollars because they believe the Fed is independent, policy decisions are made on data, not orders and inflation will be controlled when needed.

If that belief weakens, everything changes:

- Currency confidence drops
- Inflation expectations rise
- Trust in US dollar erodes slowly but deeply

Now there are two very different paths forward.

1. THE LIQUIDITY BOOM PATH (short-term bullish)

If political pressure wins, the Fed could cut rates faster and more than the economy normally allows.

That usually means:

- A weaker dollar
- Easier money
- More liquidity

Higher asset prices and higher risk appetite. 

This is why people say politics is becoming a form of QE. Not because money is printed instantly, but because policy is forced toward easier conditions.

And timing is strange. Powell’s term ends soon. If the next Fed Chair is seen as politically aligned, markets will start pricing easier money in advance.

Short term: Stocks will rise, crypto will benefit, liquidity will expand.

2. THE CREDIBILITY BREAK PATH (long-term dangerous)

This is the risk most people are ignoring. If Fed independence looks broken:

- The dollar weakens for more than just one trading day
- Foreign buyers trust US debt less
- Long term bond yields rise even if short term rates fall
- Inflation expectations slowly move higher

Because investors do not only care about returns. They care about stability and rules.

If the system looks political the Treasury demand will weaken, Borrowing costs will rise, the US will pay a credibility premium.

And most importantly inflation becomes harder to control.

This is not just a theory. It already happened before.

In the early 1970s:

President Nixon pressured the Fed Chair Arthur Burns to keep rates low

Short term: markets rallied and unemployment fell but then inflation hit over 12% by 1974 and stocks crashed.

The fix later required interest rates near 20% under Volcker. That caused a deep recession and unemployment near 10%

So the pattern is clear: Political pressure → short term growth → long term damage.

I just heard President Trump angrily complaining to an NBC reporter that he doesn’t want to hear another word about “affordability”. He claims that over the last ten months, everything has improved thanks to his inspired leadership. It doesn't exactly resonate.

Like many others, I’m getting fed up with the lies we’ve been hearing of late about the cost of living, inflation, and other factors that influence the American quality of life. (“Inflation is only 3 percent!” is one of them.) Here in the US Heartland, we’re  paying between 2 and 3 times as much as we did in early 2020 for nearly everything. Groceries have nearly tripled in price, and even the cost of emptying a dumpster has gone from $30 to $90.

President Trump claims there’s no inflation, but that’s a total disconnect from anything resembling reality. He should be hiding his head in shame. If the government and its bankster-corporate “partners” are going to rip us off with year after year of tremendous inflation in the low-to-mid double-digits for groceries and services - that’s about what it comes out to around here - the least they could do is stop lying about it.

But it gets worse. Just to enjoy some insult along with my injury, I hear that some little AI nebbish - Sam Altman, perhaps - is demanding a $multibillion/trillion bailout for his AI company. You see, Big Tech has a rule it lives by: “Socialize the losses, privatize the profits!” Everyone knows it, so who on Earth do these pampered geeks think they’re kidding?

One must admit that this rule has been working out for the technocratic elite in a very big way. For is a tiny handful of techie billionaires not ascending like runaway blimps, self-righteously reporting on their own immense philanthropy and altruism and pretending to be the heroic engineers of “socially beneficial” technological innovation? You bet they are! 

But there’s a problem: Big AI is presently losing money hand over fist because it uses more water and electricity to produce its product (“Total Information Awareness” for the Global Occupation Government and its corporate partners) than the product is actually worth (to anyone but the government and college essayists). So the big techies are sticking their guns in the face of Big Government, demanding that it dutifully yoke the hapless US taxpayer to the debt wagon on their behalf.

The idea is apparently that when something gets really big and gains the unstoppable economic momentum of Big AI, the government automatically becomes the insurer of last resort. After all, when it comes to AI, the government’s ability to thoroughly surveil and control the population in real time is at stake. And where would we all be without that?

Apparently, that’s not all for which we should be grateful. For as the techie billionaire elite peer out at us through the windows of their megayachts and private jumbo jets and busily cut jobs for natural-born Americans in the name of “economic efficiency”, they remind us that when it comes to working families, the government simply can’t function as the insurer of last resort. That, you see, would be a staggering blow to the “free market” and cripple the national economy, harming us all in so, so many ways! So we're on our own.

Come right down to it, there’s not really any arguing with that, is there. And let’s be honest: isn’t it reassuring to know that the national economy has nothing to do with working American families, but everything to do with a grasping gaggle of skinny little autistic nerds whose beaks, like those of the pelican, can hold even more than their bellies can? It’s a billionaire oligarchy, as close to Paradise (for them and their bankers and investors) as we ever had the right to expect!

But here’s the beauty part: taxpayers are where the buck stops for real. Precious AI nerds get bailed out, water and electricity companies get to jack up their rates amidst the outages, H-IB migrants get to have another half-dozen kids each while we can’t afford any of our own, and the debt-ridden government gets to offload the burden onto the US taxpayer. Only real Americans, whose privacy and job security have all but disappeared anyway, get kicked in the teeth! 

But let’s not complain about the natural order. That would be bad form. Why would anyone in his right mind not fall to his knees and give thanks? Show a little gratitude for the infinite wisdom of your betters, insolent swine! The slop grows shallow in the trough, and for us, there will be no relief. But at least our techie overlords are relieving themselves in it to make us feel better. 

And if you don’t like it, go eat cake.

But here's the twist - Iceland recovered faster than any other crisis-hit nation. By 2012, their economy was growing again while Europe wallowed in austerity. They prosecuted bankers instead of rewarding them, and GDP per capita soon exceeded pre-crisis levels.

The lesson? Sometimes the best cure for a financial hangover is to actually feel it, not reach for another drink.

Japan's economy is now breaking from three directions at once.

The Bank of Japan is running the most aggressive tightening in its history, and this is a central bank that has spent 25 years doing the exact opposite.

• The BOJ drained ¥23.5 trillion, about $146 billion, from the market in the quarter ending June 30. That is the largest quarterly drop of this entire QT cycle.
• Since its 2024 peak, the BOJ has shed ¥116.9 trillion, roughly $726 billion, or 15.6% of its total assets.
• It is now selling its equity ETFs and J-REITs outright. Nothing on the balance sheet is protected anymore.

The bond market is already showing the damage.

• The 10-year JGB yield hit 2.90%, the highest since September 1996. That is a 30-year high.
• It rose for nine straight sessions, the longest streak in 19 years.
• The 20-year is at 3.89%, the 30-year at 4.03%, and the 40-year at 4.055%. Both long ends are at record levels.

Inflation is now forcing the BOJ's hand.

• Japan's PPI just came in at 7.1% year over year, above the 6.8% forecast and up from 6.3%.
• The policy rate is still only 1.0%, far behind where inflation sits.
• Higher inflation means more rate hikes. More rate hikes means even less liquidity in a market that is already being drained.

That is the first problem. The second is the currency.

The BOJ has attempted small interventions over the last few days and none of them held. USD/JPY is still sitting near 162, close to a 40-year low for the yen. Japan already spent $72 to $73 billion defending it earlier this year and it did not work.

A weak yen is not a small problem. Japanese companies are going bankrupt because import costs keep rising. To actually strengthen the yen, Japan has to drain foreign reserves and hike rates harder.

Doing that risks breaking its own stock market, and something much bigger.

The yen carry trade is still estimated at $4 to $8 trillion. That money is borrowed cheaply in yen and parked in US stocks, emerging market debt, and crypto. In August 2024, a single 0.15% BOJ hike triggered an unwind that crashed the Nikkei 12.4% in one session, its worst day since 1987.

Then there is the third problem, and this one has no policy fix.

• Japan recorded 671,236 births in 2025, the lowest since records began in 1899.
• The fertility rate fell to 1.14, far below the 2.1 needed to hold a population steady.
• Deaths exceeded births by over 900,000 people for the second year in a row.
• Population has fallen from 128 million to around 123 million.
• Nearly 29% of the country is now over 65.

Debt is rising. The workforce that has to service that debt is disappearing.

Japan has the highest debt-to-GDP ratio in the world at 204.4%. Its central bank is draining liquidity, its bond yields are at 30-year highs, its currency is collapsing, and its future taxpayers are not being born.

Most people are watching the Fed. The next global shock is far more likely to start in Tokyo.
